# Geocoding {#sec-m3-geocodificacao} Geocoding is turning an address into a coordinate. It is a recurring and underrated step: the quality of the result determines the quality of everything that follows. Most of the work is not in the geocoding itself, but in **splitting the address into its fields** before it: street, number, neighbourhood, postcode (CEP), municipality and state, each in its own column. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(dplyr) library(stringr) library(sf) # default basemap for mapview(): OpenStreetMap mapview::mapviewOptions(basemaps = c("OpenStreetMap", "Esri.WorldGrayCanvas", "Esri.WorldImagery")) ``` ::: ## The `geocodebr` package `geocodebr` (ipeaGIT) geocodes Brazilian addresses using **CNEFE**, IBGE's National Register of Addresses for Statistical Purposes. Two advantages over commercial services: it is free and it runs locally, without sending addresses outside. That matters when the data are administrative and cannot leave the organisation's network. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} enderecos <- data.frame( id = 1:4, logradouro = c("Praça Cívica", "Avenida Goiás", "Avenida Afonso Pena", "Avenida Paulista"), numero = c(1, 400, 1212, 1578), cep = c("74003-010", "74005-010", "30130-003", "01310-200"), bairro = c("Setor Central", "Setor Central", "Centro", "Bela Vista"), municipio = c("Goiânia", "Goiânia", "Belo Horizonte", "São Paulo"), estado = c("GO", "GO", "MG", "SP") ) campos <- geocodebr::definir_campos( estado = "estado", municipio = "municipio", logradouro = "logradouro", numero = "numero", cep = "cep", localidade = "bairro" # in geocodebr, "localidade" is the neighbourhood ) resultado <- geocodebr::geocode( enderecos = enderecos, campos_endereco = campos, verboso = FALSE ) #> duckdb is storing downloaded extensions and secrets under ~/.duckdb: #> ℹ C:\Users\joaob/.duckdb #> This persists across sessions and is shared with the DuckDB CLI and other clients. #> ℹ Run duckdb(shared_home = FALSE) to use a temporary directory instead. #> ℹ See ?duckdb_storage for details and alternatives. resultado |> dplyr::select(id, logradouro, numero, municipio, lat, lon, precisao, desvio_metros) |> knitr::kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | id|logradouro | numero|municipio | lat| lon|precisao | desvio_metros| |--:|:-------------------|------:|:--------------|---------:|---------:|:-----------------|-------------:| | 1|Praça Cívica | 1|Goiânia | -16.68194| -49.25553|cep | 34| | 2|Avenida Goiás | 400|Goiânia | -16.67645| -49.25782|numero_aproximado | 7| | 3|Avenida Afonso Pena | 1212|Belo Horizonte | -19.92343| -43.93617|numero | 6| | 4|Avenida Paulista | 1578|São Paulo | -23.56205| -46.65565|numero | 6| ::: ::: The `endereco_encontrado` (address found) column shows **what** `geocodebr` actually found in CNEFE, which is not always what was asked for: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} resultado |> dplyr::select(id, logradouro, endereco_encontrado) |> knitr::kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | id|logradouro |endereco_encontrado | |--:|:-------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------| | 1|Praça Cívica |SETOR CENTRAL, GOIANIA - GO, 74003-010 | | 2|Avenida Goiás |AVENIDA GOIAS, 400 (aprox) - CENTRO, GOIANIA - GO, 74005-010 | | 3|Avenida Afonso Pena |AVENIDA AFONSO PENA, 1212 - CENTRO, BELO HORIZONTE - MG, 30130-003 | | 4|Avenida Paulista |AVENIDA PAULISTA, 1578 - BELA VISTA, SAO PAULO - SP, 01310-200 | ::: ::: On the first run, `geocodebr` downloads CNEFE (about 1.5 GB) to a local cache folder (`geocodebr::listar_pasta_cache()`). From then on, geocoding takes seconds. The output has the coordinates and, above all, the **type of match**: the most important information in the process. | `precisao` | What it means | Recommended use | |:--|:--|:--| | `numero` | the address exists in the register | any analysis | | `numero_aproximado` | position estimated between two known numbers | analysis by block or tract | | `logradouro` | got the street right, not the number | analysis by neighbourhood | | `cep` | got the postcode right, not the street | analysis by neighbourhood | | `localidade` / `municipio` | only the neighbourhood or the municipality is reliable | aggregations only | ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} resultado |> dplyr::count(precisao, sort = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: The `desvio_metros` column estimates the coordinate's error. Compare the four addresses: - **Avenida Afonso Pena, 1212**, in Belo Horizonte, and **Avenida Paulista, 1578** exist in the register with that number: precision `numero`; - **Avenida Goiás, 400**, in Goiânia, does not have number 400 in the register, and the point was estimated between the neighbouring numbers: `numero_aproximado`; - **Praça Cívica** was not found as a street: `endereco_encontrado` has only the neighbourhood, the municipality and the postcode, and the point fell on the postcode's centroid. All four "were geocoded", but only the first two are fit for an analysis at the plot scale. ::: {.callout-important} ## Never use the coordinate without looking at the precision An address geocoded to the municipality's centroid becomes a point in the middle of the city. If you compute accessibility or distance with that point, the result is fiction. And, worse, a fiction that looks precise. Filter by the precision level acceptable for the analysis and **report how many addresses were discarded**. ::: ## Before geocoding: splitting the fields For `geocodebr`, an address is not a text: it is a set of **columns**, one per field. That is what `definir_campos()` declares: | `definir_campos()` field | What goes in the column | Example | |:--|:--|:--| | `logradouro` | the type and name of the street, **without the number** | `Avenida Paulista` | | `numero` | only the number; `S/N`, `0` or `10A` become `NA` | `1578` | | `localidade` | the neighbourhood | `Bela Vista` | | `cep` | the postcode, with or without the hyphen | `01310-200` | | `municipio` | the name or the 7-digit IBGE code (mandatory) | `São Paulo` | | `estado` | the state's abbreviation or name (mandatory) | `SP` | There is no **complement** field: flat, room, block or "rear" do not go into the geocoding. If the complement stays stuck to the street name, it gets in the way of finding the street. And **there is no need to standardise** the addresses first. `geocode()` calls `enderecobr` internally (argument `padronizar_enderecos = TRUE`, the default): abbreviations (`R.`, `Av.`), accents, upper case and `nº` are handled by it. The work left to you is what it does not do: **put each piece of the address in its own column**. Administrative datasets usually have the address in a single column, with the complement and the neighbourhood in the middle. Municipality, state and postcode sometimes already come separately, as here: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} base <- data.frame( id = 1:4, endereco = c("R. XV de Novembro, 300 - Centro", "Av. Afonso Pena 1212 sala 5 - Centro", "Avenida Paulista, 1578, apto 51 - Bela Vista", "Rua Sete de Setembro nº 45, fundos - Centro"), cep = c("80020-310", "30130-003", "01310-200", NA), municipio = c("Curitiba", "Belo Horizonte", "São Paulo", "Curitiba"), uf = c("PR", "MG", "SP", "PR") ) ``` ::: Splitting is a job for a regular expression. This one follows the most common pattern: street, number (or `S/N`, "no number"), complement and, after a ` - `, the neighbourhood: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} separar_endereco <- function(x) { partes <- stringr::str_match( x, "(?i)^(.*?)[, ]+(?:n[º°o]\\.? ?)?(\\d{1,6}|s/n)\\b[ ,]*?(.*?)(?: - (.*))?$") data.frame( logradouro = partes[, 2], numero = partes[, 3], complemento = dplyr::na_if(stringr::str_remove(partes[, 4], "^[ ,]+"), ""), bairro = partes[, 5] ) } separados <- cbind(base, separar_endereco(base$endereco)) separados |> dplyr::select(endereco, logradouro, numero, complemento, bairro) |> knitr::kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |endereco |logradouro |numero |complemento |bairro | |:--------------------------------------------|:--------------------|:------|:-----------|:----------| |R. XV de Novembro, 300 - Centro |R. XV de Novembro |300 |NA |Centro | |Av. Afonso Pena 1212 sala 5 - Centro |Av. Afonso Pena |1212 |sala 5 |Centro | |Avenida Paulista, 1578, apto 51 - Bela Vista |Avenida Paulista |1578 |apto 51 |Bela Vista | |Rua Sete de Setembro nº 45, fundos - Centro |Rua Sete de Setembro |45 |fundos |Centro | ::: ::: The complement was split off only to get it out of the way: it does not go into `definir_campos()`. Notice also that the text is still "dirty" (`R.`, `Av.`), and that is fine: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} com_campos <- geocodebr::geocode( enderecos = separados, campos_endereco = geocodebr::definir_campos( estado = "uf", municipio = "municipio", logradouro = "logradouro", numero = "numero", cep = "cep", localidade = "bairro" ), verboso = FALSE ) #> duckdb is storing downloaded extensions and secrets under ~/.duckdb: #> ℹ C:\Users\joaob/.duckdb #> This persists across sessions and is shared with the DuckDB CLI and other clients. #> ℹ Run duckdb(shared_home = FALSE) to use a temporary directory instead. #> ℹ See ?duckdb_storage for details and alternatives. ``` ::: To see how much the splitting is worth, we geocode the same dataset without splitting anything, with the whole address in the street column: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sem_campos <- geocodebr::geocode( enderecos = dplyr::mutate(base, logradouro = endereco), campos_endereco = geocodebr::definir_campos( estado = "uf", municipio = "municipio", logradouro = "logradouro", cep = "cep" ), verboso = FALSE ) #> duckdb is storing downloaded extensions and secrets under ~/.duckdb: #> ℹ C:\Users\joaob/.duckdb #> This persists across sessions and is shared with the DuckDB CLI and other clients. #> ℹ Run duckdb(shared_home = FALSE) to use a temporary directory instead. #> ℹ See ?duckdb_storage for details and alternatives. dplyr::inner_join( dplyr::select(sem_campos, id, endereco, precisao_junto = precisao, desvio_junto = desvio_metros), dplyr::select(com_campos, id, precisao_separado = precisao, desvio_separado = desvio_metros), by = "id" ) |> knitr::kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | id|endereco |precisao_junto | desvio_junto|precisao_separado | desvio_separado| |--:|:--------------------------------------------|:--------------|------------:|:-----------------|---------------:| | 1|R. XV de Novembro, 300 - Centro |cep | 470|numero_aproximado | 6| | 2|Av. Afonso Pena 1212 sala 5 - Centro |cep | 275|numero | 6| | 3|Avenida Paulista, 1578, apto 51 - Bela Vista |cep | 514|numero | 6| | 4|Rua Sete de Setembro nº 45, fundos - Centro |municipio | 12818|numero_aproximado | 6| ::: ::: With the address in a single column, `geocodebr` finds no street at all: the points fall on the postcode's centroid or, without a postcode, on the municipality's, kilometres away from the address. With the fields split, all four reach the number, exact or approximate. The whole difference lies in how the columns are organised. The splitting rule is fragile: a street such as `Rua 7 de Setembro` would have the 7 read as the number, and a neighbourhood written without the ` - ` would end up in the complement. Always check a sample before geocoding the whole dataset. The case of highways (`Rodovia BR-116, km 25, s/n`) shows another limit: a highway address does not have a door number, and no urban geocoder solves it. For these, the route is different: locating by the **km** along the axis, which is a linear referencing operation. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # approximate position of km 25 along a segment ponto_km <- function(linha, km) { sf::st_line_sample(sf::st_geometry(linha), sample = km * 1000 / as.numeric(sf::st_length(linha))) |> sf::st_cast("POINT") } ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## When to standardise on your own `enderecobr`, the package `geocodebr` uses internally, can also be used directly, with one function per field. It is not needed to geocode, but it helps to **inspect** the dataset, **deduplicate** addresses or match it with another source: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} enderecobr::padronizar_logradouros(c("R. XV de Novembro", "AV. BRASIL")) enderecobr::padronizar_ceps(c("74003010", "1310200")) enderecobr::padronizar_numeros(c("0045", "s/n", "SN")) enderecobr::padronizar_bairros(c("setor central", "JD. AMERICA")) ``` ::: It makes the text uniform, but it does not split fields: `"AV. BRASIL 1200 APTO 51"` becomes `"AVENIDA BRASIL 1200 APARTAMENTO 51"`, with the number and the complement still inside the street. ::: ## Checking the result Three mandatory checks before using geocoded coordinates: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pontos <- resultado |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(lon), !is.na(lat)) |> sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4674) # 1. how many were not geocoded? c(total = nrow(resultado), geocodificados = nrow(pontos), taxa = round(nrow(pontos) / nrow(resultado), 3)) #> total geocodificados taxa #> 4 4 1 # 2. did they fall in the declared municipality? arquivo <- "dados/brutos/muni_br.gpkg" if (!file.exists(arquivo)) { br <- geobr::read_municipality(code_muni = "all", year = 2022, simplified = TRUE, showProgress = FALSE) sf::st_write(br, arquivo, quiet = TRUE) } muni <- sf::st_read(arquivo, quiet = TRUE) conferencia <- pontos |> sf::st_join(muni |> dplyr::select(code_muni, name_muni)) |> dplyr::mutate(bate = stringr::str_to_upper(name_muni) == stringr::str_to_upper(municipio)) dplyr::count(sf::st_drop_geometry(conferencia), bate) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # 3. visual inspection: the step people skip and should not mapview::mapview(pontos, zcol = "precisao", layer.name = "Precision") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Check 2 is the most valuable: an address that "was geocoded successfully" but fell in another municipality is an error that goes unnoticed in any aggregate statistic. And it shows up immediately in this count. ## Reverse geocoding The opposite route, coordinate to address, is also in `geocodebr`. The input is an `sf` object of points: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} coords <- data.frame(id = 1:2, lon = c(-49.2733, -46.6333), lat = c(-25.4284, -23.5505)) |> sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4674) geocodebr::geocode_reverso(coords, verboso = FALSE) |> sf::st_drop_geometry() |> knitr::kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | id|estado |municipio |logradouro | numero|cep |localidade | distancia_metros| |--:|:------|:---------|:----------------|------:|:---------|:-------------|----------------:| | 1|PR |CURITIBA |RUA DO ROSARIO | 160|80020-110 |SAO FRANCISCO | 6.748981| | 2|SP |SAO PAULO |RUA SANTA TERESA | 25|01016-020 |CENTRO | 43.162883| ::: ::: In practice, the most common use of reverse geocoding in transport is not getting the address, but **assigning the zone**: given a GPS point, which census tract, neighbourhood or traffic zone is it in? That is a spatial join, and you already know how to do it: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pontos |> sf::st_join(zonas, join = st_within) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## About versions `geocodebr` is recent and its interface still changes between versions. Argument names and output columns may differ. Run `?geocodebr::geocode` and `utils::packageVersion("geocodebr")` before reusing code from tutorials, including this one. The logic (split the fields, geocode, check the precision, validate spatially) is what does not change. ::: With the addresses turned into checked points, we have the first input of any routing: **from where and to where**. The second is missing: **along what**, the road network on which trips take place. That is what module 4 downloads from OpenStreetMap and prepares (@sec-m4-osm).
